'''Jedi Knights Trading Card Game''' (''Jedi Knights TCG'') is a ''Star Wars'' collectible card game published by Decipher in 2001. It was Decipher's third ''Star Wars'' card game, after the Star Wars CCG and [[Young Jedi]], and is set in the original trilogy.<ref name="sfw">Lee Bates, [http://www.scifi.com/sfw/issue199/games.html Jedi Knights Trading Card Game (review)], ''Science Fiction Weekly'', SciFi.com (2001). Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20071211183732/http://www.scifi.com/sfw/issue199/games.html Internet Archive]</ref> The game was designed by Tom Lischke and others, and all its card art is computer generated.<ref name="pyr">[http://www.sjgames.com/pyramid/sample.html?id=2388 Pyramid Review: Jedi Knights CCG], ''Pyramid'', Steve Jackson Games (17 August 2001). Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20220110205654/http://www.sjgames.com/pyramid/sample.html?id=2388 Internet Archive]</ref> Three sets came out in 2001. Decipher stopped making the game when its ''Star Wars'' license ended at the close of 2001.<ref name="ann">[http://www.decipher.com/starwars/announcement122801.html The Star Wars Announcement], decipher.com (28 December 2001). Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20020601152726/http://decipher.com/starwars/announcement122801.html Internet Archive]</ref><ref name="icv2">[https://icv2.com/articles/games/view/983/wizards-coast-gets-star-wars-ccg Wizards of the Coast Gets Star Wars CCG], ICv2 (1 January 2002). Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20261008201620/https://icv2.com/articles/games/view/983/wizards-coast-gets-star-wars-ccg Internet Archive]</ref>

== Development ==
Jedi Knights began in late 1999 as "Classic Young Jedi", a classic-trilogy version of [[Young Jedi]]. [[Chuck Kallenbach]] built a spreadsheet converting Young Jedi characters (Ric Olié became Han Solo). The team kept adding depth to appeal to core gamers, aiming for close to Star Wars CCG depth while keeping the game quick and clear for newcomers. In early August 2000 the game left the Young Jedi engine. It cut Young Jedi's randomness, let players choose who attacks whom, and moved to rounds in which both players go through each phase together.<ref name="jkd102500">[http://www.decipher.com/jediknights/designdiary/entries/102500.html Design Diary, 25 October 2000], decipher.com. Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20001208001800/http://www.decipher.com:80/jediknights/designdiary/entries/102500.html Internet Archive]</ref> According to Kallenbach, [[Warren Holland]] told him and [[Tom Lischke]]: "We want to do something different. Come up with a design. Do something you would like." It was their first game designed from the ground up.<ref name="tfnck">Josh Radke, [http://www.theforce.net/ccg/flashback/article.asp Flashback: Chuck Kallenbach interview], TheForce.Net. Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20261010072858/http://www.theforce.net/ccg/flashback/article.asp Internet Archive]</ref>

Computer-generated art was "one of the main driving forces" behind the game, to show ''Star Wars'' "as you had never seen it before". Decipher had made CGI mockups for Young Jedi, and Jedi Knights grew out of that project. Lucasfilm was very particular about the renderings of the main characters.<ref name="tfnck" /> The Art Department started in March 2000. Art lead [[Joe Boulden]] bought models from 3D fan artists in eleven countries, which covered about a third of the need, and commissioned the rest.<ref name="jkd102500" /> The game also borrowed collecting features from sports cards, such as foil stamping and First Day of Printing.<ref name="tfnck" />

Decipher announced the game at Gen Con in August 2000.<ref name="dolan">Patrick Dolan, [https://grognard.com/info1/gencon00.txt GenCon report], Usenet post (16 August 2000), copy on grognard.com. Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20250321101014/https://www.grognard.com/info1/gencon00.txt Internet Archive]</ref> It came out on 25 April 2001.<ref name="pc" />

=== A third Star Wars card game ===
Asked about the challenges of a third ''Star Wars'' card game, Kallenbach recalled that marketing was difficult and "product differentiation was much harder than with YJ".<ref name="tfnck" /> Reporting from Gen Con 2000, Patrick Dolan asked: "Are we going to have to suffer through a new Star Wars CCG every year? ... Don't they have any faith in their existing Star Wars games?"<ref name="dolan" /> When Decipher lost the license, Holland said a Wizards of the Coast game would be a fourth ''Star Wars'' trading card game, "totally incompatible with any of our existing games". He said it would arrive "at a very weak time for the Star Wars license".<ref name="icv2" />

=== Star Wars CCG crossover ===
The design team came from Decipher's other card games. In early 2001 Lischke was spearheading the design of both the Star Wars CCG and Jedi Knights. Kallenbach had worked on the Star Wars CCG and was the main Young Jedi designer.<ref name="jkpersonae" /> Playtesters included Star Wars CCG World Championship qualifiers [[Clint Hays]] and [[Steven Lewis]].<ref name="jkrules" /><ref name="trando-iv9">[http://www.trandosite.mcmail.com/iv9.htm Clint Hays interview], [[Trandosite]] (8 September 2000). A starter deck held 60 cards and a rulebook and cost $11.95; an 11-card booster cost $3.29.<ref name="pyr" /> Scum and Villainy had gold and silver foil-stamped cards at random. Its First Day of Printing boosters swapped a common or uncommon for a foil, so a pack could hold two rares.<ref name="exp" />

== Gameplay ==
Players build a deck around a theme hero and add characters, starships and events. Each game is fought over four planets, shown on two-sided location cards. Control of a planet is decided every two turns. A player who takes three planets wins. At two planets to one, both sides meet on the last planet in a Final Conflict, which goes on until only one side remains.<ref name="sfw" />

Force cards fuel the game. The Force card a player picks each turn decides the order of play, the resources available and the player's hand size.<ref name="sfw" /> Turns are simultaneous within a looping structure.<ref name="pyr" /> The destiny draw returns from the Star Wars CCG.<ref name="sfw" /> In multiplayer games, two teams of two face each other.<ref name="sfw" /> Decipher later announced 2–6 player games for Scum and Villainy.<ref name="exp" />

Most rares (and the starter-deck Blaster Rifles) come in "L" and "R" versions. The two have the same game text, but their art is shot from slightly different angles, so a pair seen side by side forms a 3-D image.<ref name="pc" />

=== Rules changes ===
Decipher replaced the Rulebook's response-timing rule (page 23), which let the player with the higher Force number respond first. Under the new rule the opponent always gets the first chance to answer with an Event, and responses then alternate. For example, if your weapon shot has +2 to hit and your opponent passes, you can play ''I Have You Now'' for +4. Your opponent can still answer with ''Camouflage'' to cancel the bonuses.<ref name="pc" /> Admiral Motti • Fleet Admiral (Premiere 70 U) received errata for balance.<ref name="pc" />

== Organized play ==
In May 2001 Decipher announced a Jedi Knights World Championship for November with a $10,000 prize for the winner.<ref name="exp" /> The November convention was cancelled in October 2001; see [[2001 Decipher World Championship]].

== Reception ==
Lee Bates of ''Science Fiction Weekly'' called the game "a solid, refreshingly fast-paced system that looks great". He praised the computer-generated art and found the stereoscopic cards "a bit gimmicky" but "undeniably cool".<ref name="sfw" /> ''Pyramid'' said the looping turn structure "will force many players to keep one hand on the rule book for their first few games". It added that fans of complex card games would find it "an enjoyable challenge". It found many human characters looked "like the famous actors, but more like their weird uncles".<ref name="pyr" />

== End of the game ==
Lucasfilm moved the ''Star Wars'' trading card game license to Wizards of the Coast. Decipher announced the change on 28 December 2001.<ref name="ann" /><ref name="icv2" /> In early March 2002 Cards Inc. bought Decipher's final stock of most Jedi Knights items, and by late April Decipher had sold out of all its ''Star Wars'' products.<ref name="icv2b">[https://icv2.com/articles/games/view/1351/decipher-star-wars-wind-up Decipher Star Wars Wind-up], ICv2 (29 April 2002). Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20261013173913/https://icv2.com/articles/games/view/1351/decipher-star-wars-wind-up Internet Archive]</ref>
